chapter: Morrison's, the Slipper and leaving music
title: Union resolution against signing contracts and Shreveport job lost
summary: Asked about a 1928 union resolution, he recalls a Shreveport contract that fell through because he refused to join the union.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Oh. Well, anyway, did you have much trouble with musicians that would sign up and leave or something? I noticed that there was a resolution made to the union by you. You know, they passed some law that musicians couldn't sign a contract unless they could fulfill it. You don't remember anything about that, huh? That was... Leave? Yeah. Yeah, that was in the union records. You've forgotten it. That was 1928.

Oh, listen, I know what they're talking about. I had a contract for, I believe it was two months or six months or something like that in Shreveport. I wanted to join the union. They told me I had to join the union. I said, okay. I went to sign the papers, you know. Some, they got messing around. Some kind of way got me mad. I told them where they could go and I left. And I went to Shreveport, but they didn't have a job. The job wasn't available.
The job wasn't an entry for? No.
Because he didn't get into the union. I didn't join the union.
Oh, yeah. Well, I didn't need the union.
Why did you spend all that money for the union? Well, that's not what he's talking about. That one. He's asking your mind. Is that at one time you were in the union and you made a resolution?
Oh, yeah. That's a resolution. I don't know what that is.
That musicians shouldn't sign a contract unless they can fulfill it.
